body.en: Probability measures the long-run relative frequency of an event. It underpins all statistical inference by describing how variable sample statistics are relative to the true population parameter.

\[0\le P(A)\le1,\quad P(\Omega)=1,\quad P(A^c)=1-P(A),\]\[P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B),\quad P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}.\]

Independent events: \(P(A\cap B)=P(A)\cdot P(B)\) (equivalently, \(P(A\mid B)=P(A)\)).

Mutually exclusive events: \(P(A\cap B)=0\Rightarrow P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B).\)

For a discrete RV \(X\) with probability distribution \(P(X=x_i)=p_i\):

\[\mu_X=E(X)=\sum x_i\,p_i,\qquad\sigma_X^2=\text{Var}(X)=\sum(x_i-\mu)^2\,p_i.\]

Linear combinations: \(\mu_{aX+b}=a\mu_X+b;\quad\sigma_{aX+b}^2=a^2\sigma_X^2.\)

For independent \(X,Y\): \(\mu_{X+Y}=\mu_X+\mu_Y;\quad\sigma_{X+Y}^2=\sigma_X^2+\sigma_Y^2.\)

\[P(X=k)=\binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k},\quad\mu=np,\quad\sigma=\sqrt{np(1-p)}.\]

CONDITIONS (BINS): Binary outcomes only; Independent trials; fixed Number \(n\) of trials; constant Success probability \(p\).

Normal approximation: valid when \(np\ge10\) and \(n(1-p)\ge10.\)

label.en: ● Sampling distribution of \(\bar{x}\) — Central Limit Theorem

body.en:
\[\mu_{\bar{x}}=\mu,\quad\sigma_{\bar{x}}=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\quad(\text{standard error}).\]

CLT: For \(n\ge30\) (or smaller if population is Normal), \(\bar{x}\) is approximately \(N\!\left(\mu,\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right)\) regardless of population shape.

Sampling distribution of \(\hat{p}\): \(\mu_{\hat{p}}=p,\;\sigma_{\hat{p}}=\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}\); approx Normal when \(np\ge10\) and \(n(1-p)\ge10.\)

caption.en: Sampling distribution of the sample mean $\bar{x}$ for $n = 25$ coffee bags ($\mu = 340$ g, $\sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{8}{\sqrt{25}} = 1.6$ g). The shaded left tail represents $P(\bar{x} < 337) = P(Z < -1.88) \approx 0.0304$.

label.en: ▲ AP Exam Traps & Pitfalls — Probability & Distributions

body.en:
• What the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) Actually States: The CLT guarantees that the sampling distribution of the sample mean \(\bar{x}\) approaches normality as sample size increases (\(n \ge 30\)). It does NOT make the population distribution normal, nor does it make the data in your sample normal!
  • Variances Add, Standard Deviations NEVER Add: For independent random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), \( \text{Var}(X - Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y) \) (variability increases even when subtracting!). Therefore, \( \sigma_{X-Y} = \sqrt{\sigma_X^2 + \sigma_Y^2} \). Writing \( \sigma_{X-Y} = \sigma_X - \sigma_Y \) is a fatal error.
  • Standard Deviation vs. Standard Error: \( \sigma \) describes individual spread in the population; \( \sigma_{\bar{x}} = \sigma / \sqrt{n} \) describes the variability of sample averages across repeated samples. Multiplying the sample size by 4 cuts the standard error in half.
  • Binomial vs. Geometric: Binomial requires a fixed number of trials \(n\) and counts successes. Geometric has no fixed \(n\) and counts trials until the first success occurs (\( P(Y = k) = (1-p)^{k-1}p \)).

body.en:
A multiple-choice test has 10 questions, each with 4 options. A student guesses randomly. Find the probability of getting (a) exactly 4 correct, (b) at least 3 correct.

\(X\sim B(10,0.25)\).

(a) \(P(X=4)=\binom{10}{4}(0.25)^4(0.75)^6=210\times0.00391\times0.1779\approx0.1460\).

(b) \(P(X\geq3)=1-P(X\leq2)=1-[P(0)+P(1)+P(2)]\approx1-0.5256=0.4744\).

Bags of coffee have weight \(\mu=340\) g and \(\sigma=8\) g. A store buys cases of 25 bags. What is the probability the mean weight \(\bar{x}\) of a case is less than 337 g?

By CLT: \(\bar{X}\sim N\!\left(340,\dfrac{64}{25}\right)=N(340,2.56^2)\).

\[P(\bar{X}<337)=P\!\left(Z<\frac{337-340}{1.6}\right)=P(Z<-1.875)\approx0.030.\]

question.en: A disease affects 5% of a population. In a random sample of 200 people, let \(X\) be the number with the disease. (a) State the exact distribution. (b) Find the mean and SD. (c) Using the normal approximation, find \(P(X\geq15)\).

solution.en: (a) \(X\sim B(200,0.05)\). (b) \(\mu=10\), \(\sigma=\sqrt{9.5}\approx3.08\). (c) Normal approx with continuity correction: \(P(X\geq14.5)=P\!\left(Z\geq\dfrac{4.5}{3.08}\right)=P(Z\geq1.46)\approx0.072\).

question.en: Independent random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) represent weights of two package components. \(X\) has mean \(\mu_X = 14\) oz and standard deviation \(\sigma_X = 2\) oz. \(Y\) has mean \(\mu_Y = 6\) oz and standard deviation \(\sigma_Y = 1.5\) oz. Let \(D = X - 2Y\). Calculate the mean \(\mu_D\) and standard deviation \(\sigma_D\) of \(D\).

solution.en:
Mean: \(\mu_D = \mu_X - 2\mu_Y = 14 - 2(6) = 14 - 12 = 2\) oz.

Standard deviation: Since \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, variances add with squared coefficients: \(\sigma_D^2 = \text{Var}(X) + (-2)^2\text{Var}(Y) = 2^2 + 4(1.5^2) = 4 + 4(2.25) = 4 + 9 = 13\). Therefore, \(\sigma_D = \sqrt{13} \approx 3.61\) oz.

question.en: The weight of checked luggage on a major airline is strongly skewed right with mean \(\mu = 42\) pounds and standard deviation \(\sigma = 12\) pounds. A commercial flight carries 64 randomly selected checked bags. (a) Describe the shape, mean, and standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean weight \(\bar{x}\). (b) What is the probability that the total weight of the 64 bags exceeds 2,800 pounds?

solution.en:
(a) Sampling distribution: Since \(n = 64 \ge 30\), by the Central Limit Theorem the sampling distribution of \(\bar{x}\) is approximately Normal despite the population skewness. The mean is \(\mu_{\bar{x}} = 42\) pounds, and the standard error is \(\sigma_{\bar{x}} = \dfrac{12}{\sqrt{64}} = 1.5\) pounds.

(b) Probability: A total weight over 2,800 pounds is equivalent to an average bag weight over \(\dfrac{2,800}{64} = 43.75\) pounds. Standardizing: \(z = \dfrac{43.75 - 42}{1.5} = 1.17\). Thus \(P(\bar{x} > 43.75) = P(Z > 1.17) = 1 - 0.8790 = 0.1210\) (approx. 12.1%).
